----- Ben-Home [NONE] 2026-10-26T23:02:30Z
The part that looks like the real defect is the missing re-discovery trigger, not the fallback itself.

Splitting what you observed into three separate conditions helps when arguing for a fix:

1. The fallback fired on a 503 or timeout. Per the 2025-03-26 authorization spec, the default endpoints exist for servers that do not expose metadata discovery at all, which is an absence signal (404 on the well-known paths), not a transport failure. A 503 says come back later, so retrying against a guessed endpoint converts a few hours of planned downtime into a durable misconfiguration.
2. It replaced metadata that had already been discovered successfully. Discovery worked at connect time, so the client had the authorization server token endpoint in hand. A refresh path that re-runs discovery should prefer the cached result and only overwrite it on a 200 that names a different issuer.
3. It is never undone. That is the part that turns an outage into a manual reconnect. A provisional endpoint needs a provenance marker and an expiry, and the next refresh should re-run discovery before using a provisional endpoint a second time.

What you can ship on your side today, without waiting for the client fix: serve the protected resource metadata and the authorization server metadata from something that stays up when the authorization server does not. Both documents are static JSON. Put them behind a long max-age on the MCP host edge, or a CDN in front of it. During the maintenance window discovery then keeps succeeding, the refresh gets its 503 from the advertised token endpoint, and the fallback condition never becomes true. Serving last-known-good metadata from the MCP host origin also makes `https://<mcp-host>/token` a harmless no-op if the fallback does fire, because you can rewrite that one path to the authorization server token endpoint at the proxy.

This failure class is not specific to one client. We run a multi-connector OAuth layer (corpusiq.io) where a connector keeps its own authorization state per account, and the same shape appears whenever a refresh target is cached as a side effect of a failed attempt: the retry logic looks healthy and the connector stays broken until someone disconnects it. The durable fix on both sides is to treat a cached fallback endpoint as a hint that expires, never as configuration.

One more line worth putting in the report: the refresh token stayed valid at the authorization server the whole time, so a refresh scheduler that retries 5xx with jitter across the maintenance window recovers with zero user action. That is a small client change and it removes this class of permanent breakage entirely. The 2025-11-25 spec dropping default endpoints is a strong argument that the fallback should not outlive a single failed request.

No request reached the server, not to the MCP endpoint and not to any well-known document. That means the failure is raised before any network egress, so the "Couldn't verify the server" result is not a judgement about your metadata. It is the same client-side step reporting twice. `Failed to clear pre-existing credentials for this URL` names a credential record keyed by the URL, and it is emitted before discovery runs, so whatever CIMD document you publish cannot be reached while that record exists.

A test that costs nothing: serve the same endpoint under a second hostname (a CNAME, or a hosts entry pointing a new name at the same address) and add it as a new connector. A credential record keyed by URL cannot exist for a URL that has never been used, so if the new URL gets past the clear step and reaches your logs, the stale record on the original URL is the blocker and your discovery chain is fine. If the new URL fails identically at the same point, the problem is not URL-scoped and the report should say so.

The 7-day lifetime result plus the registration counts change what the server-side evidence points at. If the access token now lives a week and Desktop still asks for a full sign-in, the expiry path is not what is dropping the user, and a grant keyed on a client registration that gets replaced would produce exactly the pattern you measured: refreshes that reach you and return 200, plenty of 401s in between, and 53 of 80 hosted-connector users holding more than one registration while the loopback control group sits at 2 of 15.

That is worth testing before the token lifetime is relaxed further. If the hosted connector re-runs DCR after it loses or discards its stored client data, every new registration gets a new client_id, and if grants are stored per client_id, the refresh token from the previous registration becomes unreachable to the client even though it is still valid on your side. The client then presents the old access token, gets a spec-correct 401 invalid_token, and has no refresh path it recognises, which is a Reconnect prompt. Sessions that still hold the live registration refresh normally, which is the 200s you see.

Three measurements from the OAuth store would settle which one it is:

1. For each of the 401s, resolve the presented credential to the registration that issued it, and check whether that registration is still the newest one for that user at that moment. If most 401s land on superseded registrations, the trigger is client-side re-registration, not token expiry.
2. Order the events per user: registration created, 401, token POST. If registration always precedes the 401 burst, refresh is never skipped, it is simply unusable because the grant belongs to a client the server no longer maps.
3. Hash the access token value on each 401 and each issued token, and see whether a 401 ever carries a token issued after the last refresh. That separates "no refresh attempted" from "refreshed, then kept sending the old token", which the timing pairs alone cannot.

If the re-registration reading holds, the lever on your side is grant lifetime rather than token lifetime: keep grants (or at least refresh tokens) reachable for a grace window after a registration is superseded, or key them on (user, redirect_uri) instead of client_id, so a client that comes back with a new registration can still refresh. Our own remote MCP gateway at corpusiq.io made the same trade, and we found that making the token longer hides an identity problem that returns as soon as a client updates.

Your 246-byte refresh POSTs are a useful control either way: they show the refresh grant is accepted end to end by the same library, so the failure is on the path that decides whether to call it, not in the resource server.

97:A remote JWKS is fetched under the same `global_fetch_strictly_public` protection as the metadata document, with a 64 KB limit and a 10 second timeout. It is cached in memory for 5 minutes, so a key the client removes can verify assertions until the cache expires. An unknown `kid`, or a signature that fails against the cached key, refetches it at most once every 30 seconds. A rotated key is picked up without letting bad assertions make this server hammer the client's host. Replay markers are kept in `OAUTH_KV` under `client-assertion-jti:` (see [storage-schema.md](../storage-schema.md)). Failures return a generic `invalid_client`, and `onError.internal` carries `reason: 'client_assertion_invalid'` with the specific check in `detail.reason`.

102-
103-Set `clientRegistrationEndpoint` to enable RFC 7591 Dynamic Client Registration:
104-
105-```ts
106-clientRegistrationEndpoint: '/oauth/register';
107-```

129-The implicit grant (`response_type=token`) is not supported: OAuth 2.1 removed it, and MCP clients use the authorization code flow with PKCE.
130-
131:The provider owns `tokenEndpoint`. It exchanges authorization codes for tokens, refreshes access tokens, and handles RFC 7009 revocation. Refresh tokens rotate on use. The immediately previous token remains valid until its replacement is first used, allowing a client to retry after losing a refresh response.
132-
133:A grant expires `refreshTokenTTL` seconds after the code exchange (30 days by default) however often it is refreshed. Set `refreshTokenIdleTTL` to make that lifetime slide instead: each successful refresh moves the expiry to that many seconds later, so a grant lives while the client keeps using it and expires once idle. `tokenExchangeCallback` can return `refreshTokenIdleTTL` to set the lifetime for one refresh, which lets a Worker that proxies an upstream OAuth service match the lifetime of the upstream refresh token it just rotated. See [Advanced configuration](advanced-configuration.md#token-and-client-lifetimes).
134-
135-## Resources and token audiences
136-
137-An authorization server may register one or more protected resources. Each resource has one canonical `resourceMetadata.resource`: an absolute HTTPS URI without a fragment, with lowercase `https` and a lowercase host, and an RFC 3986-safe producer serialization. Userinfo, default ports, dot-segment paths, and an empty path before a query are rejected because `Request` would rewrite them before RFC 9728 comparison. A bare origin is the only empty-path exception; use `/` before a query. Query components are supported but discouraged by RFC 9728.
138-
139-For local development, `http` is accepted for resources, `authorization_servers`, the explicit `OAuthAuthorizationServer` issuer, and absolute endpoint URLs only when the host is a loopback address (`localhost`, `127.0.0.0/8`, `::1`), so `wrangler dev` works at `http://localhost:8787`. Any other host must use `https`: Workers are always served over `https`, and OAuth 2.1 requires it. A local MCP client's loopback redirect URI is unaffected by this rule; it is governed by the RFC 8252 loopback handling described under client registration.
140-
141-Every authorization grant and access token is bound to exactly one registered resource. A central authorization server can therefore issue separate Calendar and Drive tokens from one KV namespace, but it never turns those into one multi-audience bearer token. Completing a new authorization for Drive does not replace the same user and client's Calendar grant.
142-
143-Conforming MCP clients are required to send `resource` in authorization and token requests. Resource selection and compatibility work as follows:
--
146-- When it has multiple registered resources, an authorization request must identify exactly one of them. Set `defaultResource` on `OAuthAuthorizationServer` only when older clients that omit `resource` should be routed to a deliberate compatibility default.
147-- An authorization-code or refresh-token request may omit `resource`; the server inherits the resource already stored on the grant. If present, it must match that grant and cannot retarget it.
148:- Malformed, unknown, or multi-valued resource input returns `invalid_target` before code consumption, callbacks, refresh rotation, or storage writes.
149-
150-ASCII case differences in the URI scheme and host are accepted, but port, path, trailing slash, and array cardinality remain strict. A client may also name the URL it uses at the resource when that URL adds query parameters the resource does not constrain, such as `https://mcp.example.com/mcp?mode=direct` for `https://mcp.example.com/mcp`: the protected route already accepts the resource's tokens there and points its `401` at the resource's metadata, so the authorization server maps the value to the resource (RFC 8707 §2.2). The query parameters a query-bearing resource names must be present, and when several resources cover a value the one with the most query parameters wins; a tie is rejected. Stored grant and token audiences, and `validateToken`'s resource argument, stay exact. The authorization server always stores and returns the configured lowercase scheme-and-host spelling. The token response includes the selected resource, and the access-token audience contains that resource alone.
151-
152-Token exchange cannot change the resource. Both the subject-token audience and any explicit requested resource must resolve to the same registered canonical value. A token is exchanged by the client its grant was issued to unless `tokenExchangeCallback` returns `allowCrossClientExchange: true`. Internally and externally validated tokens are accepted at a protected route only when their audience matches that route's resource.
153-
154-Path-aware API validation uses path-boundary prefix matching. A canonical audience for `https://example.com/mcp` covers `/mcp` and `/mcp/tools`, but not `/mcp-other`. A canonical trailing slash remains significant.
155-
156-## Scopes and step-up authorization
157-
158-Three places carry scopes on the wire. Two share the name `scopes_supported`, because RFC 8414 and RFC 9728 each define one, but they mean different things:

Steven: Desktop connector (not the ⟦ctxlayer⟧ notice) asks to reconnect at least daily. Live = `6bf9e6b` (sliding logins live).

**Ruled out (job_runs, 10–12 nights):** grant-idle-prune revoked 0, oauth-client-prune deleted 0; no `invalid_grant`/`Invalid refresh token`/`invalid_client` in Workers Logs; 401 on /mcp has spec-correct `WWW-Authenticate` with resource_metadata.

**Evidence (Workers Logs pasted by Steven, Nov 5–8):** every `/oauth/token` call = 200. Two client populations: Anthropic backend (`python-httpx/0.28.1`, 160.79.106.x, Columbus) = hosted connector (Desktop/claude.ai); `Bun/1.4.4` from EU IPs = Claude Code. Body length 246 = refresh_token grant, 450 = authorization_code (only ONE new Anthropic login in ~3 days). `401 invalid_token` on /mcp clusters are followed seconds–minutes later by a 246-byte Anthropic refresh (e.g. 401s 12:09→13:09:16, refresh 13:09:28) ⇒ the connector does NOT refresh on 401; the user's Reconnect click triggers a refresh that succeeds silently.

**How to apply:** don't hunt server-side OAuth bugs for this symptom. Lever = `accessTokenTTL` (library default 1h) in `oauth/provider-config.ts` — prompts drop to ~once per TTL; revocation unaffected (KV delete + per-request user recheck); keep it < MCP_LOGIN_IDLE_DAYS. content.text:
You were right: my first pass only skimmed the last few comments. I have now read every comment on #228, #1194, #1166, #1169, #1224, #1225 and #1274, and two workarounds other operators used fit ctxlayer and are not in place. Neither is confirmed as your cause yet, and nothing is built or deployed.

## Workarounds that apply to us

| Source | What others found | Their workaround | ctxlayer today |
|---|---|---|---|
| #1169 | After one transient failure during refresh or discovery, Claude switches to default endpoints on the MCP host (`/token`, `/register`, `/authorize`) and never re-discovers. | Alias those root paths to the real endpoints; stuck connectors recovered. | Unhandled on `mcp.yukitools.dev`: `POST /token` returns 405, `POST /register` 405, `GET /authorize` serves the SPA. |
| #1194, #1169 | Claude uses its published client identity (CIMD) instead of dynamic registration when the server offers it; one operator reports CIMD sign-in "refreshes normally". | Advertise CIMD support. | Off (`client_id_metadata_document_supported: false`). The library option exists: `clientIdMetadataDocumentEnabled`. |
| #1194 | Claude sends two concurrent refreshes with the same refresh token; the one whose token it keeps can be the invalidated one, and a refused refresh is terminal. | Replay the winner's rotation for 1–24 h instead of returning `invalid_grant`. | Our library only keeps the immediately previous token valid, so the race can bite. Not seen in the logs we read earlier. |
| #1166 | Same shape as ours: Desktop/Cowork, healthy OAuth, a new registration on every reconnect, large tool list. | A commenter suggested returning the existing client for identical registration metadata; nobody reported trying it. | Not done; weakest lead. |

The first row matters most: our earlier log reads were filtered to `/oauth/token` and `/mcp`, so hits on the root paths would never have shown up.

## Workarounds that do not apply

- **Entra scope-on-refresh facade** (most of #228): we are our own authorization server and refreshes return 200.
- **HTTP/2 header casing, client auth on refresh:** already ruled out or not our setup.
- **Own app deleting the connector's session** (the Supabase case): I checked; only admin suspend/delete and the nightly sweeps revoke grants, and the sweeps revoked 0 in the Nov 8 check.

## What I could not do

The classifier blocked my prod read, so I could not check the logs or your login chain since Nov 9. Two things you can run:

- **Workers Logs:** filter `mcp.yukitools.dev`, user agent `python-httpx`, path exactly `/token`, `/register` or `/authorize`, last 7 days. Any hit confirms the #1169 fallback.
- **Login chain** (read-only, prints id prefixes and timestamps for your user):

```bash
bash /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-stevenn-Projects-satisa-ctxlayer/4e4de319-72bf-4be9-82f6-2bf86f23f5bf/scratchpad/grant-chain.sh
```

## Recommendation

Build the root-path aliases and CIMD together. The aliases are harmless even if the log check comes back empty. CIMD changes how every hosted connector identifies itself at its next sign-in (existing logins keep working), so it gets a test pass before release. I would hold the rotation replay until the logs show an `invalid_grant`.

content.text:
The chain rules out every refresh-related workaround: since Nov 9 the connector has never refreshed once, yet it re-registered and forced a full sign-in seven times.

## What the rows say

- **Since the 7-day tokens went live (Nov 8 evening):** every login has `created` equal to `last refresh`. The connector held an access token valid for a week, never needed the token endpoint, and still came back with a new client id on Nov 9, 10, 11 (three times), 12 and 14.
- **Before November:** logins lasted days to weeks (Oct 12 → Oct 29, Sep 29 → Oct 10). From Nov 3 they shrink to two days, then one, then less.
- **Claude Code control** (`JizYCK`): one login since Oct 12, still healthy.

(The script's date filter was off by a year, which is why you see rows back to September; it didn't affect the reading.)

## What that does to the workaround list

| Workaround | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Rotation replay for concurrent refreshes (#1194) | Ruled out: no refresh happens at all. |
| Root-path aliases for the fallback (#1169) | Not the trigger here, since the fallback starts from a failed refresh. Still cheap insurance. |
| Longer access tokens | Already done; the chain shows it didn't help. |
| CIMD | The only lever left. The connector throws away its client registration and tokens together; with CIMD there is no registration to lose. |

The Nov 3 onset lines up with other reports in the tracker dated Nov 2–4 (#1224, #1214, one commenter says "since about 2026-11-02"). That points to a change on Anthropic's side rather than anything we shipped; our last deploy before that was Oct 12.

## Recommendation

Build CIMD support plus the aliases and release it for a test. It is a bet, not a proven fix: if the connector also discards its tokens under a stable client id, the morning sign-in stays. The evidence for it is that Claude picks CIMD over dynamic registration when offered (#1194) and one operator reports CIMD sign-ins holding where the registered ones did not.

If CIMD doesn't stop it, the fallback is to use the local `ctxlayer` entry on your machine (the Claude Code path, which has held one login since Oct 12) rather than the hosted connector.

content.content:
compatibility_date = "2026-04-01"
# nodejs_compat: stdlib shims (`crypto`, `buffer`, etc.) we rely on
#   in the agents SDK + workers-oauth-provider.
# global_fetch_strictly_public: enables CIMD (Client ID Metadata
#   Document) lookups in workers-oauth-provider so it can validate
#   DCR-registered clients without re-fetching from internal IPs.
compatibility_flags = ["nodejs_compat", "global_fetch_strictly_public"]

50-- The resource must not sit inside `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource`.
51-
52:In 0.x the metadata document was derived per request when `resourceMetadata` was omitted. In 1.x the resource is the identity every token is bound to, so it can't be implicit. Upgrading from 0.x, the value isn't a free choice: it must be the one your users' grants already carry.
53-
54-### Match the resource your existing grants carry (1.0)
55-
56-Every grant and access token stores the `resource` the client sent when the user signed in, and the client sends that same value again on every refresh. 1.x compares both against the configured resource exactly. Configure a different value, even one that covers the same paths, and every existing session breaks at once:
57-
58-| Request from an existing session          | Response                                                                                                                                        |
59-| ----------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
60-| An API call with its current access token | `401 invalid_token`, internal reason `token_audience_unbound`                                                                                   |
--
143-### Redirect URIs must be HTTPS or loopback HTTP (1.2)
144-
145:Redirect URIs must use `https`, or `http` on `localhost`, `127.0.0.0/8` or `::1`, with no userinfo or fragment. That's what MCP and OAuth 2.1 require. Every authorization request is held to it. A registration (dynamic registration, `createClient()`, `updateClient()`) needs at least one redirect URI that follows it, and may list others next to it, as Cursor lists `cursor://…` beside its https and loopback callbacks; so may a CIMD document. A request that uses one of those is refused. Registrations still refuse dangerous schemes such as `javascript:`, fragments and userinfo.
146-
147-Because it applies at authorization too, clients registered before 1.2 are held to it. A client with a remote `http` redirect URI gets a locally rendered `invalid_request` ("Invalid redirect URI") and is never redirected. It has to register a compliant URI.
148-
149-Native apps that use RFC 8252 private-use schemes (`com.example.app:/oauth/callback`) keep working if you opt in:
150-
151-```ts
152-new OAuthProvider<Env>({
153-  // …
--
216-- Grant and response types must be ones the server implements, so `grantTypes: ['implicit']` throws `Unsupported grant_type: implicit`.
217-- Redirect URIs follow the [redirect URI policy](#redirect-uris-must-be-https-or-loopback-http-12).
218:- `updateClient()` refuses a Client ID Metadata Document client while CIMD is enabled (`Client ID Metadata Document clients are updated by changing their document`). Its metadata lives in its document.
219-
220-Since 1.1, `updateClient()` also leaves clients created with `createClient()` permanent. It used to give them `clientRegistrationTTL`.
221-
222-### Type changes (1.0)
223-
224-| 0.x                                                 | 1.x                 |
225-| --------------------------------------------------- | ------------------- |
226-| `ExchangeTokenOptions.aud?: string \| string[]`     | `aud?: string`      |

/**
 * Single source of truth for the OAuthProvider config.
 *
 * `index.ts` constructs the live provider; admin tooling (e.g. the
 * OAuth-clients viewer) constructs a read-only `OAuthHelpers` instance
 * via `getOAuthApi(opts, env)` and MUST use the identical KV+path
 * config so the helpers point at the same data the live provider
 * wrote. Extracted here so we can't drift.
 *
 * The `defaultHandler` is plumbed through as a parameter because
 * helpers paths (listClients, lookupClient, etc.) never invoke it —
 * admin code can pass a stub, while `index.ts` passes the real Hono
 * app.
 */

import type { ExportedHandler } from '@cloudflare/workers-types'
import type {
  OAuthProviderOptions,
  TokenExchangeCallbackOptions
} from '@cloudflare/workers-oauth-provider'
import { McpSessionDO } from '../mcp/session-do'
import type { Env } from '../env'
import { mcpResourceUrl } from '../util/mcp-host'
import { stampTokenExchange } from './login-activity'

const NOOP_HANDLER: ExportedHandler<Env> = {
  fetch: () => new Response('not used by admin helpers', { status: 500 })
}

/**
 * Access-token lifetime: 7 days, not the library's 1 h default.
 *
 * Claude's hosted connector (Desktop / claude.ai) does not refresh when an
 * expired access token gets a 401 on /mcp — it shows the user a "Reconnect"
 * prompt, and that click is what runs the (succeeding) refresh_token grant.
 * With 1 h tokens every idle gap longer than an hour cost a prompt (2026-11
 * field finding: 401 bursts on /mcp, each followed only by a refresh after
 * the user acted, never a server-side rejection). A longer token makes the
 * prompt roughly weekly at worst.
 *
 * Why this is safe here: access tokens live in KV, so suspend/delete
 * (`revokeAllUserGrants`) still kills them instantly, and the session DO
 * re-checks user status on init. The cost is a longer useful life for a
 * leaked bearer. Must stay well below `MCP_LOGIN_IDLE_DAYS` so an active
 * client always refreshes inside the idle window.
 */
export const MCP_ACCESS_TOKEN_TTL_SECONDS = 7 * 24 * 60 * 60

/**
 * A login lasts as long as it keeps refreshing (see oauth/login-activity.ts).
 *
 * Both TTLs below are passed as `undefined` on purpose — the library then
 * writes the grant and the DCR client record to KV with NO expiration, and
 * expiry becomes ours to decide. That is the only way to get a sliding
 * session out of this library: `refreshTokenTTL` is stamped once, at the
 * authorization-code exchange, and the refresh path re-saves the same
 * absolute instant (it even refuses a `refreshTokenTTL` returned from the
 * token-exchange callback). `clientRegistrationTTL` behaves the same way
 * from the registration moment, so leaving it at its 90 d default would cap
 * the login independently — the final refresh would just fail
 * `invalid_client` instead of `invalid_grant`.
 *
 * What replaces them: `tokenExchangeCallback` stamps every exchange into
 * `oauth_grant_activity`, and the nightly `grant-idle-prune` job revokes
 * grants that have been silent for `MCP_LOGIN_IDLE_DAYS`. Instant lockout is
 * unaffected — suspend/delete still calls `revokeAllUserGrants`, and the
 * session DO re-checks user status on init.
 *
 * `env` is required: the canonical resource (below) is derived from it, and
 * admin tooling building `OAuthHelpers` from these same options (see the
 * module header) must name the identical resource. Those helpers never
 * exchange a token, so the callback being installed there is inert.
 *
 * Resource (workers-oauth-provider 1.x): every grant and access token is
 * bound to exactly one resource, compared exactly — see `mcpResourceUrl`.
 * Only `/mcp` is served. The legacy HTTP+SSE endpoint (`/sse`) was dropped
 * at the 1.x upgrade: 1.x cannot cover two sibling paths with one resource,
 * the SSE transport is deprecated in MCP, and no stored grant was bound to
 * it (2026-11 KV scan of the largest deployment: 0 of 444).
 */
export function oauthProviderOptions(
  env: Env,
  defaultHandler: ExportedHandler<Env> = NOOP_HANDLER
): OAuthProviderOptions<Env> {
  // apiHandlers requires ExportedHandlerWithFetch (Required fetch);
  // our handler carries `fetch` at the value level but its declared
  // type doesn't line up exactly, so the map is cast once.
  const apiHandlers = {
    '/mcp': McpSessionDO.serve('/mcp', { binding: 'MCP_SESSION_DO' })
  } as OAuthProviderOptions<Env>['apiHandlers']
  return {
    apiHandlers,
    defaultHandler,
    resourceMetadata: { resource: mcpResourceUrl(env) },
    authorizeEndpoint: '/oauth/authorize',
    tokenEndpoint: '/oauth/token',
    clientRegistrationEndpoint: '/oauth/register',
    // Explicit `undefined` — it overrides the library defaults (30 d / 90 d)
    // through the options spread, and is what makes the KV records
    // expiration-less. See the note above before "simplifying" these away.
    refreshTokenTTL: undefined,
    clientRegistrationTTL: undefined,
    accessTokenTTL: MCP_ACCESS_TOKEN_TTL_SECONDS,
    tokenExchangeCallback: (opts: TokenExchangeCallbackOptions) => stampTokenExchange(env, opts),
    scopesSupported: ['mcp']
  }
}

content.text:
CIMD support and the root-path aliases are built, and `bun run verify` passes (731 unit, 55 web, 537 integration). Nothing is committed or deployed.

## What changed

- **CIMD on:** the provider now accepts a client's published metadata URL as its `client_id` and advertises that in the discovery document. Dynamic registration stays available. It had never been enabled before, despite the compat flag being set.
- **Sign-in keeps earlier logins for CIMD clients:** a CIMD client id is shared by Desktop, web and mobile, so the library default of revoking the user's previous grant would sign the other surfaces out. That revoke is now skipped for CIMD clients only; the nightly idle sweep still retires unused ones.
- **Root-path aliases:** `/token`, `/register` and `/authorize` now behave exactly like `/oauth/token`, `/oauth/register` and `/oauth/authorize`.
- **Asset routing:** those three paths are added to `run_worker_first` in `wrangler.toml` and in `../ctxlayer-ops/wrangler.template.toml`. The second is in the ops repo, which I edited because yukitools renders its config from it; without it the aliases would not take effect there.
- **Admin clients viewer:** CIMD logins have no stored client record, so the viewer now adds a row for each CIMD client that holds a login. This part has no test.

The new tests cover the aliases (register, code exchange, refresh via the root paths) and a full CIMD sign-in and refresh with nothing written to the client store.

## What is not known yet

- **Whether your existing connector switches to CIMD on its own.** One report shows an explicit "Use Claude's published identity (CIMD)" option in the add-connector dialog, so you may have to remove and re-add the connector after the release.
- **Whether a stable client id stops the connector discarding its tokens.** That only shows after a release.

## After you release

1. `https://mcp.yukitools.dev/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` should show `client_id_metadata_document_supported: true`.
2. `POST https://mcp.yukitools.dev/token` should no longer return 405.
3. Sign in once more, then rerun the login-chain script. The script prints only the first six characters of the client id, so a CIMD login shows as `https:`. If the morning prompts then stop, the bet paid off.

The main files are [provider-config.ts](apps/worker/src/oauth/provider-config.ts), [default-endpoints.ts](apps/worker/src/oauth/default-endpoints.ts), [cimd.ts](apps/worker/src/oauth/cimd.ts) and [complete-mcp.ts](apps/worker/src/idp/complete-mcp.ts).
